And so, having been harassed and oppressed, we saw the city of Massilia <note>modern Marseille, which sided with Pompey and was besieged by Caesar</note> paraded in a triumph as an example of lost empire, the city from which our commanders once triumphed after wars beyond the Alps. I could mention many other crimes against our allies, if the sun had ever seen anything more unworthy than this single act. We are therefore justly punished. For unless we had borne their unpunished crimes, such unbridled license would never have reached a single man. From him, the inheritance of private property came to a few, and the inheritance of greed came to many wicked men.

Indeed, the seed and cause of civil wars will never be absent as long as desperate men remember that bloody spear and hope for it again. For when Publius Sylla <note>a relative of the dictator Sulla</note> had brandished it while his relative was dictator, thirty-six years later he did not shrink from an even more criminal spear. Another man, who had been a clerk during that first dictatorship, was city quaestor in this one. From this it must be understood that while such rewards are offered, civil wars will never end. And so, only the walls of the city stand and remain, and even these now fear the most extreme crimes; but we have utterly lost the Republic itself. And it is into these disasters that we have fallen. 

For we must return to the point: as long as we preferred to be feared rather than to be dear and loved. If these things could happen to the Roman people for ruling unjustly, what should individuals think?

### <insert>On attaining affection</insert>

But since it is clear that the power of goodwill is great, and that of fear is weak, it follows that we should discuss by what means we can most easily obtain that affection we desire, joined with honor and trust. But we do not all <note>require it in the same way</note>

<summary>Cicero argues that Rome's civil wars and the loss of the Republic resulted from a shift from benevolent leadership to rule by fear and greed. He illustrates this through the mistreatment of allies like Massilia and the recurring cycle of property confiscations.</summary>
